newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden seen waiting with EMU despite Riksbank view.
newsitem.headline: Sweden seen waiting with EMU despite Riksbank view.

text.p: Sweden's influential central bank has thrown its weight behind early membership of a single EU currency but economists still expect the country to wait before joining, reflecting public and political scepticism.

Swedish membership of economic and monetary union (EMU) from the start in 1999 "is not totally ruled out even if the probability is relatively low," said economist Ake Gustafsson at Swedbank in Stockholm.
Gustafsson and other economists believe Sweden will decide to wait and see with EMU, not taking part from its launch but leaving the door open for possible membership a few years later.
"I believe (the government) will want to try and keep it open to join in the second wave," said chief economist Carl B Hamilton at Handelsbanken.

Last week, Prime Minister Goran Persson reiterated that the decision on whether to join EMU was "still an open question" even though the country would meet the Maastricht treaty's economic qualifying criteria.

His ruling Social Democrats are due to decide its position at a party congress in September and parliament will make the final decision in October or November -- just a few months before EU leaders are due to rule on which countries can join.
Persson stressed that a decision on EMU must be anchored in Swedish society.

"And if I should judge now from the Swedish opinion, it's a negative decision. But you don't know. Much can happen and it is still an open question," he told a press conference while on an official visit to Luxembourg.

He has called for a wide public debate on membership but the cabinet has cooled considerably because of opinion polls showing strong public distaste for monetary union. Over the last weeks, ministers have expressed differing views on the benefits of EMU.

But the powerful Riksbank, rejecting the conclusions of an official inquiry into Swedish EMU membership, which it said had underestimated the benefits to the country, said last Friday Sweden should be among the first wave to join in January 1999.
"Our possibility to have an impact on the development of the Union would be less if we stayed outside," Riksbank Governor Urban Backstrom said.

The Riksbank said an official report by Professor Lars Calmfors published last year, which concluded that the risks of EMU membership were severe and that Sweden should not be among the first to join, was over-cautious.
Handelsbanken's Hamilton said the Riksbank statement was a "fairly scathing criticism" of the Calmfors report and that it would diminish its value as a basis for decision.
"But I don't think this will really influence the government's decision about not joining in the first wave in 1999," he said.
Hamilton said, however, that the clear position of the Riksbank increased the chances of Sweden joining in a second wave in 2001 and also paved the way for a more open and sound debate about EMU.

Hamilton, advocating early membership, said it was important to be in EMU from the start, partly as it was then that it would be decided how the future European Central Bank would operate its monetary policy.
"I don't think the arguments that we must stay out because of employment reasons are well founded," he added.
